title: The Screen Has to Earn Its Time
author: What Teachers Have to Say
source: What Teachers Have to Say (Substack), September 15, 2026
summary: A teacher-writer argues that 'too much screen time' is really several different, conflated problems, too much sitting, devices crowding out conversation, low-thought tasks, and that counting minutes, as with a mandated IXL platform, measures none of them. Illustrating with two visually identical laptop-using students who are doing very different intellectual work, the piece proposes starting from the specific thinking a lesson requires, then choosing whether and how a device serves that thinking, citing the CyberSandwich protocol's capture-compare-develop structure and both the UK's Education Endowment Foundation and UNESCO's technology-adoption guidance. It concludes that the operative question is never how long a screen was open, but what became possible while it was.
points: Argues 'screen time' conflates several distinct problems (sedentary time, crowded-out conversation, low-cognitive-demand tasks) that need different responses.
Uses a required IXL platform example to show how time-based compliance can coexist with zero actual learning.
Presents the CyberSandwich protocol's capture-compare-develop structure as an example of technology serving a defined thinking sequence rather than replacing one.
Cites EEF and UNESCO frameworks that require naming the learning purpose before adopting a tool.
Offers a four-sentence audit teachers can run on any existing digital activity.
quotes: My frustration begins when the clock becomes the entire argument, because students can clock the minutes and still avoid looking at the lesson.

Imagine two students with laptops open. One is moving through a sequence of questions, looking for whichever answer lets them continue. The other has written a response, compared it with a partner's, and is deciding how to explain a disagreement. The devices look similar from the hallway. The intellectual work could be very different.
As Adam Moler put it describing this process, "The magic isn't in the steps. It's in what happens between them." That "between" is where the screen has to earn its time.

The Education Endowment Foundation's guidance on digital technology asks schools to establish the teaching and learning purpose before introducing the tool, and to plan the support needed to use it well. That is a much more demanding test than whether a resource looks modern.
The important question is not simply, "How long was the screen open?" It is, "What became possible while it was open?
